title: hot-tenant-throttle-and-driver-memleak-synthesis
content:
Summary:
We observed a gradual quality-of-service (QoS) degradation across one Dedicated GPU pool over a 36-hour window. Symptoms: rising p90 inference latency, increased request queuing, and sporadic Pod evictions without correlated host-level CPU saturation. Root cause hypothesis is a combination of a driver memory leak on a subset of nodes and an overly aggressive scale-in parameter in the pool autoscaler that amplified the impact during a scheduled nightly drain.

Impact:
- Affected pool: europe-west1-gpu-pool-3 (NVIDIA A100s, mixed tenancy)
- Customer-facing latency: p90 increased from ~120ms to ~420ms for certain text-generation routes
- Error surface: transient 503s during scale/eviction windows for ~8% of requests to that pool
- Window: 2025-11-07 02:10 UTC -> 2025-11-08 14:30 UTC (36+ hours of degraded tail latency)
- Business impact: several mid-market customers reported degraded UX; no data loss.

How we detected it (signals):
- Grafana alert: pool-level tail-latency alert firing intermittently (p90 > 300ms)
- Autoscaler logs: repeated rapid scale-in events during the nightly drain window
- Node exporter: growing GPU driver memory footprint (non-application GPU memory) on 6/48 nodes
- K8s events: increased Pod eviction spikes correlated with the same nodes
- Per-tenant token queue depth metric spiking for a handful of heavy tenants (hot-tenant bursts)

Initial timeline (high level):
- 2025-11-07 00:00 UTC: scheduled maintenance window begins — automated pool drain job kicked off in europe-west1
- 2025-11-07 02:05 UTC: first tail-latency alert, oncall paged
- 2025-11-07 02:20 UTC: SRE starts triage: observed evictions and rising driver memory; hypothesis space: noisy tenant vs driver issue
- 2025-11-07 03:10 UTC: applied temporary mitigation: disable aggressive scale-in on the pool (increase cool-down to 20m)
- 2025-11-07 05:00 UTC: tail latency improved briefly but returned later as nodes continued to degrade
- 2025-11-08 08:00 UTC: reproduced memory growth by running a synthetic workload replay on an affected node in staging -> consistent leak observed against driver version 535.77
- 2025-11-08 12:00 UTC: rolled forward driver build with mitigation patch to a canary set of nodes (driver 535.82-rc), no immediate regressions
- 2025-11-08 14:30 UTC: pool stabilized after rolling patch + tuned autoscaler settings

Investigation notes / evidence collected:
- Node GPU memory (non-kernel) increased by ~4GB over 18 hours on affected hosts while application GPU usage stayed constant
- coredumps absent; kernel logs showed repeated nvml handle timeouts before driver memory increase
- The pool autoscaler had a scale-in grace period of 5m and permissive threshold for reclaiming underutilized nodes — combined with nightly drain, it removed nodes faster than the asymptomatic degradation could tolerate
- A small set of tenants produced high, bursty allocation patterns; the autoscaler removed the nodes they were on which caused remaining nodes to absorb load and pushed latency above SLOs

Hypothesis / root cause (synthesized):
1) A GPU driver regression (version 535.77) causes gradual GPU-side memory leakage in a common codepath used by inference runtime warm-up. The leak is slow and only visible after many hours of allocation churn.
2) The autoscaler runbook/parameters are tuned for fast recovery but aggressive for scale-in (5m cool-down). During the nightly drain+scale-in, nodes with the leak were decommissioned faster than expected, causing churn: remaining capacity absorbed 'hot tenant' bursts and saw tail latency spikes.
3) The interaction of (1) and (2) produced a domino: slow resource degradation -> autoscaler removes nodes -> tenant storms concentrated -> queueing and tail latency degradation -> more evictions perceived as failures.

Immediate mitigations applied during incident:
- Increased autoscaler scale-in cool-down to 20m for the affected pool (temporary)
- Suspended the scheduled drain job for the entire cluster for 6 hours to allow controlled canary remediation
- Scoped routing: moved high-throughput tenants off europe-west1-gpu-pool-3 into a warm standby pool to relieve burst pressure
- Deployed patched NVIDIA driver to a canary subset and monitored driver mem usage before rolling to remaining nodes

Longer-term fixes and proposals:
- Driver: pin stable driver version for dedicated pools until driver team certifies the new release. Add driver mem usage to the node-level SLA dashboard and alert if non-application GPU memory increases > 1GB/hour.
- Autoscaler: add safety gating for pools with node-level degrading signals. Suggested changes:
  - scale-in cool-down default -> 15m (instead of 5m)
  - require sustained underutilization for two consecutive evaluation cycles before scale-in
  - add a soft hold when maintenance/drain jobs are active
- Scheduling/routing: implement a 'hot-tenant isolation' policy: when a tenant's allocation rate exceeds X per minute, automatically route new allocations to standby capacity rather than the same pool.
- Observability: more granularity on per-node driver metrics (nvml handle errors, allocation churn), and a synthetic long-run workload in staging to catch slow leaks (8–24 hour replay).

Runbook snippet for oncall (to add to dedicated-pools-runbook):
- If p90 tail-latency rises > 300ms and k8s evictions observed:
  1) Check node-level GPU "driver-mem-nonapp" metric for upward trend; identify top-5 nodes by delta
  2) If >3 nodes show >2GB growth in 6 hours, suspend automated drains and increase scale-in cooldown to 30m
  3) If tail-latency persists after step 2, move top heavy-tenants to standby pool and enable extra burst capacity for 30m
  4) Open a channel with infra/driver team and include nvml logs + dmesg from affected nodes

Dashboards / alerts to create/update:
- Node driver non-app memory growth (iso: bytes/hour)
- Autoscaler rapid-scale-in alert (fires if >N nodes removed within M minutes)
- Hot-tenant allocation rate alert (per-tenant allocation QPS sustained > threshold for 10m)
- Synthetic long-run leak test health (staging job status)

Open action items (owners + ETA):
- Aisha: coordinate driver rollback pin across dedicated pools (ETA: 2025-11-14)
- Lin: implement autoscaler gating PR (GH-rlw/infra#4123) and perf test in staging (ETA: 2025-12-01)
- Diego: build hot-tenant routing prototype and run it in shadow for 2 weeks (ETA: 2025-12-08)
- Infra team: run full fleet driver validation (cross-region) and publish a compatibility matrix (ETA: 2026-01-10)

Notes to self / lessons learned (informal):
- Slow degradations are sneaky — our alerting focused on immediate capacity signals, not slow resource leakage. We need to think in terms of 'health slope' not just instantaneous thresholds.
- Autoscalers can make problems worse if they act on signals that are downstream symptoms. Add more upstream signal checks before destructive actions.
- The hot-tenant pattern will keep biting us unless there is automatic isolation. Manual moves work but are slow in ops hours.

Related tickets / follow-ups:
- JIRA-SRE-981: autoscaler gating work
- GH-rlw/infra#4123: autoscaler param PR (draft)
- JIRA-DRIVER-44: driver regression repro and patch tracking

Appendix: quick commands used during triage (for reproducibility):
- top offending nodes: kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector=status.phase!=Succeeded | grep europe-west1-gpu-pool-3
- GPU mem usage: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.total --format=csv -l 60
- nvml error logs: journalctl -u nvidia-driver | grep -i nvml | tail -n 200

If anything is missing here that helped you in triage, paste into this doc. This is intentionally a synthesis so we can convert to a formal postmortem later.
